findings.note: Real and deliberate. hc/settings.py:68 is `SECRET_KEY = envsecret("SECRET_KEY", "---")`, so an instance deployed without the SECRET_KEY environment variable signs its sessions with three hyphens. That is not a key an attacker has to steal -- healthchecks publishes it, as `Default: ---`, in its own configuration documentation, so anyone can forge a session for any user on such an instance without ever seeing the source. Healthchecks also documents that the value 'should be set to a unique, unpredictable value', which makes this a knowing convenience for local development rather than an oversight. Firm rather than certain because a real deployment normally does supply the variable.

Real and deliberate. hc/settings.py:70 is `DEBUG = envbool("DEBUG", "True")`, so a deployment that does not set the DEBUG environment variable runs with DEBUG on. Healthchecks knows this: its own production checklist in README.md tells operators to 'make sure it is set to False'. Convenient for local development, a hazard for anyone who deploys without reading the checklist, which is exactly what this rule is for. Reported at tentative because the environment can override it.

A genuine gap, not a configuration choice. Healthchecks never assigns SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE and, unlike DEBUG or SECRET_KEY, offers no environment variable for it either, so there is no supported way for an operator to turn it on short of patching settings.py. The project clearly expects a TLS-terminating proxy -- it reads SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER from the environment at line 78 -- but a proxy does not set this flag, and without it a browser that touches the plain-HTTP URL even once transmits the session cookie in clear text on the wire. Firm rather than certain only because we cannot see the deployment; the absence of the setting itself is not in doubt.

Correct about the source and defensible in practice. Healthchecks reads SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER from the environment, which says plainly that the intended deployment puts a TLS-terminating proxy in front, and such a proxy is the normal and better place to perform the HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect -- doing it in Django means the plain-HTTP request has already reached the application. This is precisely the case the rule reports at tentative rather than firm, because we cannot see the proxy from inside the repository. Unlike the two cookie flags above, delegating this one loses nothing.
